              Rohingya community members gather before a television at Jamtoli Camp 15, Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh as they await the International Court of Justice’s final judgment in the genocide case against Myanmar, November 19, 2026.

As the International Court of Justice in The Hague delivered its judgment on November 19 in the landmark case that Gambia brought against Myanmar for violating the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide, thousands of Rohingya waited anxiously in refugee camps in Bangladesh.  In the Jamtoli Camp 15 in Cox's Bazar District, many crowded around a television. About two hours into the reading of the judgment, it started to rain. But no one moved.The court’s president spoke in English, a language rarely heard in the crowded camps where over a million Rohingya sought refuge after fleeing Myanmar military attacks in 2017. At 5:13 p.m. local time, a community leader relayed the court’s ruling in the Rohingya language to the waiting crowd, telling them that, by nine votes to six, the court found Myanmar “committed genocide against the Rohingya group in northern Rakhine State.” The crowd clapped and cheered; many were in tears.“The Myanmar military tried to convince the world that we had lied,” said 58-year-old Monajat Alam, from Rathedaung Township. “Today, the truth has been recognized.”The ruling was based on evidence showing that thousands of Rohingya civilians, including children, had been killed and that there was widespread sexual violence and destruction of villages during the 2017 military campaign. The court found the evidence also showed that Myanmar intended to destroy a substantial part of the Rohingya population.Nemat Hussen from Maung Nu in Buthidaung Township, where Myanmar soldiers massacred hundreds of Rohingya villagers on August 27, 2017, brought along his son. Maung Nu was one of three villages that Gambia asked the court to examine for evidence of genocidal intent.“In 2017, I lost my mother and eldest son,” Nemat Hussen said. “Since that day, I’ve been waiting for justice, and today I brought my son to hear the judgment.”The court ordered Myanmar to investigate suspected perpetrators of genocide and prosecute them where warranted, compensate the Rohingya for the harm they suffered, and facilitate the safe, voluntary, and dignified return of those displaced, among other measures.“Today, my hopes have grown tremendously,” Monajat Uddin said. “I wish that we’ll be able to return to Rakhine and live in peace and our homeland will be safe so that we can return.”
articles.content:
Click to expand Image Rohingya community members gather before a television at Jamtoli Camp 15, Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh as they await the International Court of Justice’s final judgment in the genocide case against Myanmar, November 19, 2026. © 2026 Human Rights Watch

As the International Court of Justice in The Hague delivered its judgment on November 19 in the landmark case that Gambia brought against Myanmar for violating the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide, thousands of Rohingya waited anxiously in refugee camps in Bangladesh.

In the Jamtoli Camp 15 in Cox's Bazar District, many crowded around a television. About two hours into the reading of the judgment, it started to rain. But no one moved.

The court’s president spoke in English, a language rarely heard in the crowded camps where over a million Rohingya sought refuge after fleeing Myanmar military attacks in 2017. At 5:13 p.m. local time, a community leader relayed the court’s ruling in the Rohingya language to the waiting crowd, telling them that, by nine votes to six, the court found Myanmar “committed genocide against the Rohingya group in northern Rakhine State.”

The crowd clapped and cheered; many were in tears.

“The Myanmar military tried to convince the world that we had lied,” said 58-year-old Monajat Alam, from Rathedaung Township. “Today, the truth has been recognized.”

The ruling was based on evidence showing that thousands of Rohingya civilians, including children, had been killed and that there was widespread sexual violence and destruction of villages during the 2017 military campaign. The court found the evidence also showed that Myanmar intended to destroy a substantial part of the Rohingya population.

Nemat Hussen from Maung Nu in Buthidaung Township, where Myanmar soldiers massacred hundreds of Rohingya villagers on August 27, 2017, brought along his son. Maung Nu was one of three villages that Gambia asked the court to examine for evidence of genocidal intent.

“In 2017, I lost my mother and eldest son,” Nemat Hussen said. “Since that day, I’ve been waiting for justice, and today I brought my son to hear the judgment.”

The court ordered Myanmar to investigate suspected perpetrators of genocide and prosecute them where warranted, compensate the Rohingya for the harm they suffered, and facilitate the safe, voluntary, and dignified return of those displaced, among other measures.

“Today, my hopes have grown tremendously,” Monajat Uddin said. “I wish that we’ll be able to return to Rakhine and live in peace and our homeland will be safe so that we can return.”
articles.reasoning: The International Court of Justice ruling recognizing Myanmar's genocide against the Rohingya is a landmark legal and moral victory with broad significance for justice and human rights globally. It provides tangible hope for accountability, reparations, and safe return for a large displaced population, with detailed context and direct impact on millions.
articles.personality_title: International court rules Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – In 2017, Myanmar’s military attacked the Rohingya people, a Muslim minority group in northern Rakhine State. Over a million Rohingya fled to refugee camps in Bangladesh to escape violence and killings. Gambia brought a case against Myanmar to the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in The Hague, accusing the country of genocide under an international treaty.

**What happened** – On November 19, 2026, the ICJ announced its judgment. After careful review, the court decided by a vote of nine to six that Myanmar did commit genocide against the Rohingya. The ruling was based on evidence of mass killings, sexual violence, and village destruction in 2017. Refugees in camps in Bangladesh listened closely as the verdict was shared in their own language, bringing tears and applause.

**Impact** – This ruling is important because it officially recognizes the suffering of the Rohingya and holds Myanmar responsible under international law. The court ordered Myanmar to investigate and punish those responsible, pay compensation to victims, and help the displaced Rohingya return home safely. This is a rare moment where justice is being demanded for a group that has faced severe violence and denial.

**What's next step** – Myanmar must now follow the court’s orders to investigate and prosecute the genocide. The Rohingya and the international community will watch closely to see if Myanmar takes action. The ruling also encourages efforts to support safe returns of Rohingya refugees and to rebuild their communities.

**One-sentence takeaway** – The International Court of Justice has officially found Myanmar guilty of genocide against the Rohingya, marking a key step toward justice and accountability for the victims.
articles.personality_title_fr: La Cour internationale de justice déclare le Myanmar coupable de génocide contre les Rohingyas
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – En 2017, l'armée du Myanmar a attaqué les Rohingyas, une minorité musulmane dans l'État de Rakhine au nord. Plus d'un million de Rohingyas ont fui vers des camps de réfugiés au Bangladesh pour échapper à la violence et aux massacres. La Gambie a porté plainte contre le Myanmar devant la Cour internationale de justice (CIJ) à La Haye, accusant le pays de génocide selon un traité international.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Le 19 novembre 2026, la CIJ a rendu son jugement. Après examen, la Cour a décidé à neuf voix contre six que le Myanmar avait commis un génocide contre les Rohingyas. Le verdict s’appuie sur des preuves de tueries massives, violences sexuelles et destructions de villages en 2017. Les réfugiés au Bangladesh ont écouté attentivement la décision traduite dans leur langue, avec des larmes et des applaudissements.

**Impact** – Ce jugement est important car il reconnaît officiellement les souffrances des Rohingyas et tient le Myanmar responsable au regard du droit international. La Cour a ordonné au Myanmar d’enquêter, de punir les coupables, d’indemniser les victimes et d’aider les Rohingyas déplacés à rentrer chez eux en toute sécurité. C’est un moment rare où la justice est demandée pour un groupe victime de violences graves et de déni.

**Prochaine étape** – Le Myanmar doit désormais suivre les ordres de la Cour pour enquêter et poursuivre les auteurs du génocide. Les Rohingyas et la communauté internationale surveilleront de près les actions du Myanmar. Ce jugement encourage aussi les efforts pour soutenir le retour sûr des réfugiés et la reconstruction de leurs communautés.

**Une phrase clé** – La Cour internationale de justice a officiellement reconnu le génocide commis par le Myanmar contre les Rohingyas, marquant une étape importante vers la justice et la responsabilité.
articles.personality_title_es: La Corte Internacional de Justicia declara que Myanmar cometió genocidio contra los rohinyás
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – En 2017, el ejército de Myanmar atacó al pueblo rohinyá, una minoría musulmana en el norte del estado de Rakhine. Más de un millón de rohinyás huyeron a campos de refugiados en Bangladesh para escapar de la violencia y asesinatos. Gambia presentó un caso contra Myanmar ante la Corte Internacional de Justicia (CIJ) en La Haya, acusando al país de genocidio según un tratado internacional.

**Qué pasó** – El 19 de noviembre de 2026, la CIJ anunció su fallo. Tras revisar el caso, la corte decidió por nueve votos contra seis que Myanmar cometió genocidio contra los rohinyás. La decisión se basó en pruebas de asesinatos masivos, violencia sexual y destrucción de pueblos en 2017. Los refugiados en Bangladesh escucharon atentos el veredicto traducido a su idioma, con lágrimas y aplausos.

**Impacto** – Esta sentencia es importante porque reconoce oficialmente el sufrimiento de los rohinyás y responsabiliza a Myanmar según el derecho internacional. La corte ordenó a Myanmar investigar y castigar a los responsables, compensar a las víctimas y ayudar a los rohinyás desplazados a regresar a casa de forma segura. Es un momento poco común en que se pide justicia para un pueblo que ha sufrido violencia grave y negación.

**Próximo paso** – Myanmar debe cumplir ahora con las órdenes de la corte para investigar y enjuiciar el genocidio. Los rohinyás y la comunidad internacional estarán atentos a las acciones de Myanmar. La sentencia también impulsa esfuerzos para apoyar el regreso seguro de los refugiados y la reconstrucción de sus comunidades.

**Una frase clave** – La Corte Internacional de Justicia ha declarado oficialmente a Myanmar culpable de genocidio contra los rohinyás, marcando un paso clave hacia la justicia y la rendición de cuentas.

articles.title: No government approval needed to form or join a group, UN rights committee says
articles.summary: People do not need their government’s permission to form or join an association, the UN Human Rights Committee said on Thursday, issuing new guidance as civic space shrinks around the world.
articles.content:
General Comment No. 38 sets out how Article 22 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights should be interpreted. Article 22 guarantees the right to freedom of association.

The guidance comes at a time when civil society groups, human rights defenders, trade unions, political parties and grassroots movements face growing legal and administrative hurdles.

Freedom of association allows people to come together voluntarily – including at work – to pursue shared goals. The committee called it a cornerstone of democracy and essential to the enjoyment of other rights.

Tweet URL

‘A crucial barometer’

“Attacks and infringements on the right to freedom of association are thus a crucial barometer of a broader crackdown on human rights, the rule of law and democracy,” it said.

“The right to freedom of association is not conditioned by a State’s authorisation or acknowledgement. This means that no prior authorisation is needed for its enjoyment and exercise.”

The committee stressed that people must be free to choose whether to form or join registered or informal associations, a decision that “rests solely with the individuals themselves”.

Simply joining or belonging to an unregistered association “must not be criminalised or sanctioned”, it added.

Dissent and protest protected

The right also covers ideas and activities that may be seen as “controversial, dissent or disruptive”, including “peaceful collective civil disobedience actions”.

The committee warned against misusing counter-terrorism and national security laws, including vaguely worded laws targeting so-called “extremist” or “undesirable” organizations.

Associations are also entitled to seek, receive and use funding, including from abroad, and to cooperate internationally “without the risk of being labelled a ‘foreign agent’ or any similar label or a threat to national security”.

No spying or infiltration

The committee also cautioned against surveillance of associations and their members, including digital surveillance, and against infiltration by undercover police or intelligence agents.

Freedom of association is not absolute. However, the committee said any restrictions must be the exception and must have a clear legal basis and a legitimate aim. They must also be strictly necessary and proportionate.

Forcibly suspending or dissolving an association should only ever be a last resort and must be subject to judicial safeguards, it added. The committee stressed that “the relation between right and restriction and between rule and exception must not be reversed”.

The UN Human Rights Committee is made up of 18 international experts who monitor how countries implement the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, which 175 States have ratified.

Members are elected by States parties for four-year terms. They are not UN staff and are not paid for their work.
articles.source: UN News - Global perspective Human stories
articles.reasoning: The UN Human Rights Committee's new guidance affirming that no government approval is needed to form or join associations is a significant advancement for freedom of association worldwide. It protects a fundamental democratic right, counters growing restrictions on civil society, and supports broad human rights and democratic governance. The detailed guidance addresses key issues like protection from criminalization, surveillance, and misuse of laws, providing a meaningful framework with broad societal impact.
articles.personality_title: UN affirms no government approval needed to join or form groups
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Around the world, people who want to join or create groups like clubs, unions, or political parties often face tough rules and government permission requirements. These rules make it harder for people to work together and share their ideas.

**What happened** – On Thursday, the UN Human Rights Committee gave new guidance saying people do not need government approval to form or join any group. This guidance explains Article 22 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, which protects the right to freedom of association.

**Impact** – This is important because it protects a basic democratic right. The committee said people should be free to join any group they want, whether it is officially registered or informal. The guidance also warns governments not to punish people for being in unregistered groups or for peaceful protests, even if their ideas are different or controversial. It also protects groups from unfair spying or false accusations.

**What's next step** – Countries that have agreed to the Covenant are expected to follow these rules. This could help people everywhere to organize more freely, defend their rights, and take part in democracy without fear of unfair restrictions.

**One-sentence takeaway** – The UN has made it clear that people everywhere have the right to freely form or join groups without needing government permission.
articles.personality_title_fr: L’ONU confirme qu’aucune autorisation gouvernementale n’est nécessaire pour rejoindre ou créer un groupe
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Dans le monde entier, les personnes qui souhaitent rejoindre ou créer des groupes comme des clubs, syndicats ou partis politiques doivent souvent obtenir des autorisations gouvernementales, ce qui complique leur organisation.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Jeudi, le Comité des droits de l’homme de l’ONU a publié de nouvelles directives affirmant que les gens n’ont pas besoin d’autorisation gouvernementale pour former ou rejoindre un groupe. Ces directives expliquent l’article 22 du Pacte international relatif aux droits civils et politiques, qui protège la liberté d’association.

**Impact** – Cela protège un droit démocratique fondamental. Le comité a déclaré que les personnes doivent être libres de rejoindre n’importe quel groupe, qu’il soit enregistré ou informel. Il met aussi en garde contre la punition des personnes pour leur appartenance à des groupes non enregistrés ou pour des manifestations pacifiques, même si leurs idées sont différentes ou controversées. Il protège également les groupes contre la surveillance injuste ou les fausses accusations.

**Prochaine étape** – Les pays ayant ratifié le Pacte devraient respecter ces règles. Cela pourrait permettre aux gens du monde entier de s’organiser plus librement, de défendre leurs droits et de participer à la démocratie sans crainte de restrictions injustes.

**Résumé en une phrase** – L’ONU rappelle que chacun a le droit de former ou rejoindre librement un groupe sans autorisation gouvernementale.
articles.personality_title_es: La ONU afirma que no se necesita permiso del gobierno para formar o unirse a grupos
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – En todo el mundo, las personas que quieren unirse o crear grupos como clubes, sindicatos o partidos políticos a menudo enfrentan reglas estrictas y necesitan permiso del gobierno, lo que dificulta su organización.

**Qué pasó** – El jueves, el Comité de Derechos Humanos de la ONU emitió una nueva guía que dice que las personas no necesitan permiso del gobierno para formar o unirse a un grupo. Esta guía explica el Artículo 22 del Pacto Internacional de Derechos Civiles y Políticos, que protege la libertad de asociación.

**Impacto** – Esto protege un derecho democrático básico. El comité dijo que las personas deben ser libres para unirse a cualquier grupo, ya sea registrado o informal. También advirtió a los gobiernos que no deben castigar a las personas por pertenecer a grupos no registrados o por protestas pacíficas, incluso si sus ideas son diferentes o controvertidas. Protege a los grupos contra vigilancia injusta o acusaciones falsas.

**Próximo paso** – Se espera que los países que firmaron el Pacto sigan estas reglas. Esto podría ayudar a las personas en todo el mundo a organizarse con más libertad, defender sus derechos y participar en la democracia sin temor a restricciones injustas.

**Resumen en una frase** – La ONU deja claro que todas las personas tienen derecho a formar o unirse libremente a grupos sin necesidad de permiso gubernamental.

articles.title: Peacekeeping: With 500 paternity and child support claims unresolved, UN scales up accountability
articles.summary: The UN is adding new accountability measures to better support children fathered by peacekeepers, the Under-Secretary-General for Management Strategy, Policy and Compliance, Catherine Pollard, announced Thursday.
articles.content:
Since 2006, the organization has received some 800 paternity and/or child support claims involving peace operations personnel in cases of sexual exploitation and abuse (SEA), the Secretary-General’s Deputy Spokesperson Farhan Haq told journalists in New York.

Children ‘left behind’

“Claims of paternity are one of the most serious consequences of SEA, and it impacts not only the victim but also the children left behind,” Ms. Pollard said.

“Their fathers have abandoned them and have left the peacekeeping mission, often before they were even born. These fathers normally do not provide child support unless they're forced to do so,” she emphasised.

While progress has been made to prevent and respond to sexual exploitation and abuse, around 500 of the claims remain unresolved, including 400 where paternity has yet to be determined, according to Mr. Haq.

Tweet URL

‘Unjust situation’

“It is an unjust situation, and we are doing everything in our power to change this, which is only something we can do together with Member States,” Ms. Pollard stressed.

Indeed, the first step in responding to paternity and child support claims is to make sure the accused peacekeeper is the biological father, which requires investigation and evidence – usually DNA paternity testing.

Member States may have to compel accused fathers to submit to these tests in line with national legislation, Ms. Pollard said.

Building on previous work

In late 2024, the UN launched a Public Paternity Dashboard, which shows the status of the resolution of child support and paternity claims involving “blue helmets”.

It shows what claims involve, how long they've been pending, and their status.

“But we thought more detail was required,” Ms. Pollard explained.

“So, we expanded the public reporting to more clearly show the status of the claims, including to clearly identify where Member States are working with us to resolve claims and where they are not.”

These assessments may inform future deployment decisions, Mr. Haq noted.
articles.source: UN News - Global perspective Human stories
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant and meaningful action by the UN to address unresolved paternity and child support claims related to sexual exploitation and abuse by peacekeepers. This initiative aims to improve accountability and support for affected children, which has broad humanitarian and societal implications. The article provides sufficient context about the problem, the scale of unresolved claims, and the concrete steps being taken, including public reporting and cooperation with member states.
articles.personality_title: UN strengthens efforts to support children fathered by peacekeepers
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Since 2006, the United Nations (UN) has received about 800 claims involving peacekeepers accused of fathering children through cases of sexual exploitation and abuse. Many of these children have been left without support because the fathers often leave before the child is born and do not provide child support.

**What happened** – The UN announced new measures to improve accountability and support for these children. Catherine Pollard, Under-Secretary-General for Management Strategy, Policy and Compliance, said the UN is working closely with member countries to resolve around 500 unresolved paternity and child support claims. These efforts include investigations and DNA testing to confirm if accused peacekeepers are the biological fathers.

**Impact** – This is important because it addresses a serious problem affecting vulnerable children who have been left behind by absent fathers. By increasing transparency with tools like the Public Paternity Dashboard, the UN hopes to ensure that more cases are resolved fairly and that peacekeepers are held responsible for their actions.

**What’s next step** – The UN will continue to push member states to cooperate in testing and resolving claims. The information gathered may also influence decisions about which peacekeepers get deployed in the future, aiming to prevent further abuse.

**One-sentence takeaway** – The UN is stepping up efforts to hold peacekeepers accountable and improve support for children born from cases of sexual exploitation and abuse.
articles.personality_title_fr: L’ONU renforce ses efforts pour soutenir les enfants issus de casques bleus
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Depuis 2006, l’Organisation des Nations Unies (ONU) a reçu environ 800 réclamations impliquant des casques bleus accusés d’avoir engendré des enfants dans des cas d’exploitation et d’abus sexuels. Beaucoup de ces enfants sont laissés sans soutien car leurs pères partent souvent avant leur naissance et ne paient pas de pension alimentaire.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – L’ONU a annoncé de nouvelles mesures pour améliorer la responsabilité et le soutien à ces enfants. Catherine Pollard, Sous-Secrétaire générale pour la stratégie, la politique et la conformité, a déclaré que l’ONU travaille étroitement avec les États membres pour résoudre environ 500 dossiers non réglés concernant la paternité et la pension alimentaire. Ces mesures comprennent des enquêtes et des tests ADN pour confirmer si les casques bleus accusés sont les pères biologiques.

**Impact** – Cela est important car cela répond à un problème grave qui concerne des enfants vulnérables abandonnés par leurs pères absents. En augmentant la transparence grâce à des outils comme le tableau de bord public de paternité, l’ONU espère que davantage de cas seront traités équitablement et que les casques bleus seront tenus responsables.

**Prochaine étape** – L’ONU continuera à encourager la coopération des États membres pour les tests et la résolution des dossiers. Les informations recueillies pourraient aussi influencer les décisions sur le déploiement futur des casques bleus, afin de prévenir de nouveaux abus.

**Une phrase clé** – L’ONU intensifie ses efforts pour rendre les casques bleus responsables et améliorer le soutien aux enfants nés de cas d’exploitation et d’abus sexuels.
articles.personality_title_es: ONU refuerza esfuerzos para apoyar a hijos de cascos azules
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Desde 2006, las Naciones Unidas (ONU) han recibido cerca de 800 reclamaciones relacionadas con cascos azules acusados de ser padres de niños nacidos en casos de explotación y abuso sexual. Muchos de estos niños han quedado sin apoyo porque sus padres suelen irse antes de que nazcan y no brindan manutención.

**Qué pasó** – La ONU anunció nuevas medidas para mejorar la responsabilidad y el apoyo a estos niños. Catherine Pollard, Subsecretaria General para Estrategia, Política y Cumplimiento, dijo que la ONU trabaja con los Estados miembros para resolver alrededor de 500 casos pendientes de paternidad y manutención. Esto incluye investigaciones y pruebas de ADN para confirmar si los cascos azules acusados son los padres biológicos.

**Impacto** – Esto es importante porque aborda un problema serio que afecta a niños vulnerables abandonados por sus padres. Al aumentar la transparencia con herramientas como el Panel Público de Paternidad, la ONU espera que más casos se resuelvan justamente y que los cascos azules sean responsables.

**Próximo paso** – La ONU seguirá insistiendo en la cooperación de los Estados miembros para realizar pruebas y resolver los casos. La información recopilada también podría influir en las decisiones sobre qué cascos azules serán desplegados en el futuro para evitar más abusos.

**Una frase clave** – La ONU intensifica sus esfuerzos para responsabilizar a los cascos azules y mejorar el apoyo a los hijos nacidos de casos de explotación y abuso sexual.

articles.title: How to turn impostor syndrome into a superpower
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 20 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03465-6A nagging sense that you don’t belong can keep you grounded and might help to improve your performance.
articles.content:
In 2021, Kwabena Boahen Asare found himself in at the deep end when he joined a skin cancer laboratory to gain hands-on research experience.

For Asare, who was a first-year undergraduate student at Dartmouth College in Hanover, New Hampshire, at the time, it was an exciting but daunting prospect. Not only was he the sole bachelor’s programme student working alongside senior researchers with years of experience under their belts, he was also the only Black person in the lab. Although Asare’s mentor and colleagues were supportive and encouraging, he felt overwhelmed and out of his depth. “There was a steep learning curve,” he says.

At the time, Asare viewed his struggles as a sign that he didn’t belong in research. This feeling was compounded by the fact that he was surrounded by colleagues who didn’t share his background as a first-generation student from Ghana.

His experience, and those of many like him, is commonly labelled as impostor syndrome — the fear of not being as competent or knowledgeable as other people think, despite objective accomplishments. In a world that often prizes unflinching self-confidence and boldness, impostor syndrome is usually cast as a psychological flaw that the individual needs to ‘fix’. But it can be a natural response to working in a challenging environment or striving towards an ambitious goal, organizational psychologists say.

Impostor syndrome can also be a reaction to systemic bias and exclusion in the workplace, particularly for people from under-represented groups, including women, says Ruchika Malhotra, an inclusion strategist and founder of Candour, a workplace consultancy in Seattle, Washington. The company advises organizations on strategies to create diverse teams and inclusive cultures. One study1 conducted at universities in the United States found that women who work in scientific fields that particularly value intellectual brilliance are more likely to feel like impostors than are their male colleagues.

How I tackled post-PhD impostor syndrome

Much of the discussion about impostor syndrome pathologizes healthy self-doubt and shifts the responsibility onto individuals instead of the environments that exclude and marginalize them in the first place, adds Malhotra. “A lot of the ways that it’s been talked about haven’t been constructive,” she says.

Although it comes with drawbacks, in some situations, impostor syndrome can be beneficial. For instance, it can help people be better prepared and more focused, particularly when they have a long to-do list.

“Impostor thoughts are almost like your superpower when things get pretty overwhelming,” says Basima Tewfik, an organizational psychologist who studies impostor syndrome at Massachusetts Institute of Technology in Cambridge.

Looking back, Asare says that his impostor syndrome prompted him to reflect on why he wanted to become a researcher in the first place. It has also made him more conscious of his resilience, how he needs to improve and when to seek help, as well as giving him more empathy. This has made him better able to support younger students and researchers who are feeling out of place. “It became my strength,” says Asare, who is now an oncology researcher and consultant at Dartmouth Hitchcock Medical Center in Lebanon, New Hampshire.

Blurry picture

Impostor syndrome was first described as ‘impostor phenomenon’ in a 1978 paper on high-achieving women2 co-authored by psychologists Pauline Clance and Suzanne Imes, both then at Georgia State University in Atlanta. They wrote that people who experience this phenomenon “maintain a strong belief that they are not intelligent; in fact they are convinced that they have fooled anyone who thinks otherwise”.

In the decades since, impostor phenomenon has morphed into a syndrome, even though it isn’t a medical diagnosis, nor is it classified as a psychiatric disorder. A review published in 20233 suggests that around 70% of people will feel unworthy of their accomplishments at some point in their lives. These feelings are even more prevalent in academia, with a 2012 study4 finding that as many as 82% of graduate students experience impostor syndrome to at least some degree. This pattern of thinking often affects high achievers and is associated with lower job satisfaction, hindered performance and burnout. Although some studies, including the 2012 paper, suggest that impostor syndrome affects mostly women and people from other groups under-represented in academia, others argue that it arises in specific situations rather than among particular groups. Relatively few studies have investigated whether commonly cited strategies, such as listing one’s accomplishments and accepting compliments from others, are actually effective.

Impostor syndrome has become a catchphrase in popular culture, with dozens of articles, books and courses describing what it is and how people can overcome it. But in the scientific literature, at least, the exact definition of impostor syndrome, or phenomenon, varies widely. This has created a murky picture of what it really is and how it affects people, says Tewfik. “There are a lot of different ways people describe this phenomenon,” she says. The loose definition has made it easy to confuse impostor syndrome, which causes people to make inferences about what other people think of them, with regular self-doubt, which is more of a personal reflection of your own capabilities, according to Tewfik.

‘Maybe I was never meant to be in science’: how impostor syndrome seizes scientist mothers

Much of the research on impostor syndrome has also used measures that have made it difficult to distinguish from other psychological patterns, such as negative affectivity, a personality trait that is linked to a tendency to experience negative emotions such as fear, anxiety and insecurity, adds Tewfik. This crossover might explain why most studies on impostor syndrome have shown only negative outcomes, such as a lack of career planning and low motivation to lead5. “It’s possible that what we’ve been studying is actually something much more akin to fear,” says Tewfik.

This overly negative slant is exacerbated by the fact that many workplaces, including academic ones, place too much emphasis on self-confidence, says Tomas Chamorro-Premuzic, an organizational psychologist at University College London. One 2024 study6 found that workers who display confidence are perceived as more competent and dominant, irrespective of their actual ability.

If impostor syndrome hinders a person’s ability to work or form relationships, it’s usually a symptom of a deeper issue or clinical condition, such as an anxiety disorder. But feeling like you’re about to be ‘found out’ before delivering a big presentation, for example, is usually a sign that you’re being challenged or working outside your comfort zone, says Chamorro-Premuzic. “There is a very healthy degree somewhere that we’re not appreciating,” he adds (see ‘A toolkit for working with impostor syndrome’).

In scientists, impostor thoughts can simply be a by-product of thinking critically and approaching things with a healthy dose of scepticism, says Samantha Sutton, an independent career coach for scientists in Boston, Massachusetts. It’s also often a natural response to working in a high-achieving, competitive environment or towards an ambitious goal and should be normalized instead of treated as a problem to solve, she adds. “If you’re up against something big, you should be scared,” says Sutton. When she communicates this to her clients, they are often relieved to hear that they don’t need to strive for total self-confidence before taking steps towards their goals. “They realize that nothing is wrong,” adds Sutton.

articles.personality_title: How feeling like an impostor can actually help you succeed
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Many people, especially in challenging jobs or school, sometimes feel like they don’t belong or aren’t good enough. This feeling is called impostor syndrome. It often happens to people who are new, from different backgrounds, or working in very competitive places.

**What happened** – Kwabena Boahen Asare, a college student from Ghana, felt this way when he started working in a skin cancer research lab. He was the only Black student and the youngest person there, so he felt out of place. But instead of giving up, he used these feelings to learn more, work harder, and help others who struggled too. Experts say that impostor syndrome isn’t always bad; it can push people to prepare better and stay focused.

**Impact** – This story shows that impostor syndrome can be a useful feeling, not just a problem. It helps people stay aware of their limits and grow stronger. It also highlights that some groups, like women and minorities, face this feeling more because of unfair treatment or exclusion. Understanding this can help workplaces become more welcoming and supportive.

**What’s next step** – Researchers and workplaces are learning to see impostor syndrome in a new way. Instead of telling people to just be confident, they want to fix the environments that make people feel left out. People like Asare continue to use their experiences to support others, making science and other fields more inclusive.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Feeling like an impostor can motivate people to improve and support others, especially when workplaces become more fair and welcoming.
